rationale: P2a built the experience register's substrate and its criteria validator; this is the write path — the only door into the register. It exists in this shape because migration 218 deliberately seeded no entries by raw INSERT: the first rows in the register are meant to be ones the register's own contract accepted, since a library whose contents never passed its own validator has no evidence the contract is enforceable at all. Three rules are the substance, and each closes a door rather than asking a person or a future step to remember something. FIRST, status is not writable: 'approved' is a council verdict and 'proven' is the first live green run of bound criteria — both are things that HAPPENED, and a writer that can assert them converts evidence into a claim. Supplying a status is an error rather than a silent no-op, because silently dropping it would let a caller believe it had approved something. SECOND, a contract change demotes: if an approved entry's contract, criteria or binding schema changes, it returns to draft, because the approval was of the old contract and carrying it forward would make 'approved' mean 'was approved of something, once'. Cosmetic fields do not demote, and comparison is on canonical JSON so key order cannot produce a phantom demotion — a spurious warning trains people to ignore the real one. THIRD, validation refuses the write and reports every problem at once, because each refusal round trip back to a writing agent is an LLM call. This submission also carries the fix for the one gap the previous council raised (corr bbdd2c5e-1b9d-4179-a31c-a8a5c3c3bf32, APPROVED with 5 advisory objections, 11 reviewers, unreadable 0): bug_historian and guardian each independently objected that an entry could defer every hard check and still reach 'approved' while asserting nothing substantive, which was also risk #5 of that submission. My answer there was 'a minimum-executable-checks rule at the approval step' — a rule somebody must remember, which is a schema defect wearing a documentation costume. Migration 230 makes it a CHECK constraint instead, so the state is unrepresentable no matter which path later writes the status. Two other objections from that round are answered here with evidence rather than argument, and reviewers should check both: there is NO pre-existing write-time criteria validator to reuse — `evaluateStaticCriteria` and `extractCriteriaFence` in the tool-acceptance checker both run at READ time, which is the failure class this addresses rather than a duplicate of it; and `subject_type='experience'` in doc_plans is 59 revisions of a SINGLE subject_key, so 'experience-pattern' fragments no travelling-doc history. Status: committed (36bb6c992) and migration 230 applied; the Go is NOT yet in a rolled image, so the write path is inert in production.

plan.summary: Add write_experience_pattern, the only action that can put a row into the experience register, and the constraint that stops a hollow entry being approved. The action validates entry shape (kebab-case name, kind against the migration's CHECK, a contract whose every trigger names an observable outcome, and no site-specific destination in a base entry), runs ValidateExperienceCriteria over the criteria template with the contract and clause documents passed as extras so a placeholder used in a contract clause but never declared is caught too, checks that every named invariant actually exists (requires_invariant is jsonb, so the database cannot), and upserts. Status is never taken from the caller; a change to a clause-bearing field demotes an approved entry back to draft inside the same transaction that reads it FOR UPDATE. Migration 230 adds executable_checks and deferred_checks to the row and a CHECK that an entry may only be non-draft with at least one executable check; the same two fields are refused from the caller, because an entry that scores itself defeats the constraint that reads the score. The travelling doc is deliberately NOT written here — it is a plain write_doc_plan step with subject_type 'experience-pattern', reusing the machinery a tool's doc already uses.

edits.rationale: The single door into the register, so that every row in it has passed the contract. Validation refuses rather than warns, and returns every problem at once. The demotion rule is the part most worth a reviewer's attention: it is the difference between 'approved' meaning 'this contract was approved' and 'some ancestor of this contract was approved once'. Reading the existing row FOR UPDATE inside the write transaction is deliberate — the demotion decision and the update must not straddle another writer.

Two clauses make a contract checkable at all. A trigger must name an observable outcome — a trigger with no `then` is how 'there is a button here' gets recorded as behaviour, which is the defect the no-inert-control invariant exists for. And a navigating trigger must name a destination ROLE, never a URL: a concrete value in a base entry is the bugs_closed/045 class, a static fallback re-applied on every render that a per-site binding cannot override. changedExperienceContractFields draws the demotion line explicitly rather than by intuition, so widening it is a decision; a field absent from a partial update counts as unchanged, because silently emptying a clause nobody mentioned would delete a rule and look like a no-op.

Closes the gap two seats raised independently and that I had named as risk #5. Deferral must stay possible — dropping a check the platform cannot execute would delete the clause from the record, which is how a pattern comes to look fully checked when its most important rule is not checked at all — but it must not be free. The constraint makes an all-deferred approval unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged, and it holds regardless of which path later writes the status. Safe ahead of the image, deliberately: both columns have defaults, the constraint only ever TIGHTENS so it cannot create 184's split-contract shape, and it constrains only states no path can currently write.

The `kind` vocabulary is the same split-contract shape as doc subject types, so it gets the same treatment: the test re-derives the allowed set from the newest migration that defines the CHECK rather than trusting a hand-maintained Go list. Proved by induced fault before commit — adding 'site-journey' to the Go list fails naming 218_experience_register_substrate.sql, which also confirms the regex matched the intended file rather than passing vacuously. The behaviour tests are pinned to HARVESTED entry fragments, not shapes invented to satisfy the validator.

plan.risks: 1. The demotion rule is the sharpest edge. If experiencePatternContractFields is drawn too wide, ordinary edits demote approved entries and the warning gets ignored; too narrow, and a clause changes under an approval that still reads as current. It is a hand-maintained list with no mechanical guard — unlike the kinds vocabulary and the checker capability table, both of which have lockstep tests. A reviewer should say whether that list can be derived instead. 2. write_experience_pattern is registered but nothing calls it yet: no workflow step names it, so it is inert until a seed does, and its rules have only test evidence. 3. The action does not write the travelling doc; a workflow that writes an entry and forgets the paired write_doc_plan step produces a register row with no provenance, and nothing currently detects that. 4. missingExperienceInvariants returns nothing when params.DB is nil rather than failing closed — pinned by a test so the contract is deliberate, but it means a caller in a DB-less context gets no invariant check rather than an error. 5. Migration 230 was applied before the image that populates its columns. I argue this is safe (defaults, tightening-only, constrained states unreachable) but that argument is mine and is exactly the kind a reviewer should test rather than accept. 6. The upsert builds its column list dynamically; a jsonb column added to the table and to experiencePatternJSONFields is written without touching the function, but a column added to the table and NOT to that list is silently never written. A test asserts every listed field is marshalled, which does not catch a field missing from the list in the first place.
